Extricate

EK-strih-kayt -- from Latin extricare ('to disentangle'), from ex- ('out of') + tricae ('hindrances, perplexities'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To extricate is to get someone or something out of a trap, tangle, or difficult situation that holds it.

Volunteers spent the better part of the afternoon working to extricate the stranded kayaker from the fallen tree blocking the river.

Worked Example

Realizing too late that the contract locked her into five more years of payments, she spent months with a lawyer trying to extricate herself from the agreement.

That effort to work your way free of something that has you tangled up or stuck -- whether physically or legally -- is exactly what it means to extricate yourself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

free: To free someone or something is the broadest word for ending any kind of confinement, and it says nothing about how. To extricate is narrower and harder-won: it means working something out of a tangle or trap that holds it, one careful step at a time.

dislodge: To dislodge something is to knock or force it out of one stuck position — a boot from mud, a ball from a gutter. To extricate involves a whole trap or tangle and a longer, more careful effort to work loose of everything holding it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

entangle: to cause something to become twisted together or trapped

ensnare: to trap someone in a difficult situation

Where it sits · how complete the freeing is — disentangle → extricate → release

disentangle vs. extricate: Disentangle is milder than extricate and less complete: you disentangle kite string from a branch one knot at a time, yet the kite may still hang in the tree, while to extricate something is to work it all the way out of whatever holds it.

release vs. extricate: Release goes further than extricate: to extricate the miners is to work them painstakingly out of the wreckage, while their release is the more absolute endpoint — completely and finally free.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-

prefix — ex-: out of (Latin)

root — tric-

root — tric-: hindrances, perplexities (Latin (tricae))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ex- ('out of') plus tricae ('hindrances, tangles') plus the verb suffix -ate. To extricate something is to work it out of a tangle of obstacles.

Use the root in a new word: intricate

Use the root in a new word: intricate: The watchmaker used a magnifying glass to examine the clock's intricate inner gears.
